title: Grok Build coding agent leaks oodles of confidential info, some belonging to SpaceXSI
content:
Grok Build, the vibe-coding agent from SpaceXSI, is leaking data—some of it proprietary business information and other sensitive secrets—from thousands of its users, including the very same Elon Musk-owned company that offers the platform, new research shows.
The information is revealed through links allowing Grok Build users to share their apps with others. Grok takes steps to randomize the URLs so only people who know the exact URL can access the data stored there. A design decision by developers of the platform, however, completely torpedoes that objective and makes it possible for anyone to enumerate thousands of live Grok Build projects. Except in rare cases, clicking those links opens the app and reveals all data associated with it.
You had one job
Research from security firm Claroc shows that the exposed data includes things like internal business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, galley checklists from a celebrity cruise line, and employee names and ID numbers. Ironically, some of the sensitive data comes from two-dozen apps built by SpaceXSI (the name of the now-merged SpaceX and xAI) itself. A small sampling of the documents revealed in the SpaceXSI apps—Claroc found 24 of them—include an onboarding plan, marked confidential, for a new member of SpaceXSI’s enterprise sales team, a sales territory map of 594 accounts, internal system addresses for sales team tools, and advertising proposals.
“We were shocked,” Claroc said in a Tuesday post. “The company that makes Grok had its own internal material open to anyone holding the link, and we had never been given it. Had the sales team bought a tool for this, it would have sat behind company sign-in, open only to the team. Built with AI, it went live open to anyone with the link.
Claroc notified SpaceXSI of the privacy spill on Sunday. When no one responded, a Claroc official took to X to tag both Musk and Grok Manager Matt Palmer about the threat. At the time this post went live almost all data remained available with one notable exception: the contents from the 24 SpaceXSI apps. All of them were exposing the information on Monday evening. SpaceXSI began removing the links within a few hours of Ars sending an email with questions for this article. At the time this post went live, links for all 24 apps returned an “app not found” error.

report.summary: Grok Build’s link-sharing design exposed thousands of users’ confidential data, including internal SpaceXSI apps, until Ars inquiry prompted removal.
report.background: AI “vibe-coding” agents let users generate and deploy full apps from prompts, often with one-click sharing. These platforms prioritize speed over security, and many rely on unguessable URLs as the only access control. That model assumes links stay secret, but if URLs can be enumerated, every shared app becomes public. The incident fits a broader pattern: AI-generated internal tools and prototypes are proliferating outside IT oversight, creating shadow apps that handle business plans, customer data, and employee records. Startups are adding sharing features to drive adoption, but authentication, authorization, and data-loss prevention are often afterthoughts. As enterprises adopt coding agents, link-sharing defaults and missing sign-in become a systemic risk, not just a bug.
key_points: Claroc found that Grok Build’s share links could be enumerated, exposing thousands of live projects. The leaked material included business plans, ad proposals, medical exam results, cruise-line galley checklists, and employee names and ID numbers—sensitive data from real users, not test fixtures.

The most awkward part: 24 exposed apps were built by SpaceXSI itself. They revealed a confidential onboarding plan for an enterprise sales hire, a 594-account sales territory map, internal system addresses, and advertising proposals. Claroc said a normal SaaS tool would have sat behind company sign-in.

The root cause was a design decision, not a sophisticated attack. Grok Build randomized URLs so only people with exact links could access apps, but the platform made projects discoverable anyway. Clicking a link generally opened the app and showed all associated data, with no authentication barrier in most cases.

Disclosure was slow. Claroc reported the leak on Sunday, got no response, and then tagged Elon Musk and a Grok manager on X. SpaceXSI began removing links only after Ars asked questions. By publication, all 24 SpaceXSI app links returned “app not found,” while other users’ data had largely remained available.

The episode highlights a broader vibe-coding risk: AI agents can ship internal tools and dashboards without security review. Teams may treat shared links as private, but without sign-in and access controls, prototypes can expose company secrets, personal data, and credentials—creating shadow IT at machine speed.
report.impact: For the AI industry, the leak undercuts the promise that coding agents can safely democratize app building. Security will become a competitive differentiator: platforms that default to private apps, require authentication, and scan for secrets will win enterprise trust. For developers, it is a reminder that URL obscurity is not access control; AI-generated apps need auth, authorization, logging, and data minimization before sharing. Regular users should assume any “share link” app may be public and avoid putting sensitive data into prototypes. Enterprises need inventory and review of AI-built apps, plus policies for link sharing. The reputational damage is amplified because the platform’s own owner exposed internal sales material, making the incident a cautionary tale for every company adopting vibe coding.
report.tools: To reduce similar exposure, watch secret-scanning and app-security tools: Gitleaks and TruffleHog for finding leaked credentials; Semgrep for static checks; OWASP ZAP and Nuclei for probing exposed endpoints and auth gaps; Keycloak or Ory for adding sign-in; Supabase Row Level Security for per-user data access. For teams using AI app builders, pair them with a pre-deploy checklist covering authentication, link-sharing defaults, and data classification.
